tip: 'Ci' replaces a place already mentioned. 'Non ci vado' means I'm not going there, with 'ci' standing for the location.
'Le' is the indirect form here: 'chiedere' takes a person with 'a' ('chiedere a qualcuno'), so 'le' means to her, not a direct them.
'Telefonare' takes 'a', so its object is indirect: 'gli telefono' means I phone him, using 'gli' and not 'lo'.
Before a vowel, both 'lo' and 'la' drop to l', giving 'l'ho già fatto' (I already did it). So 'l'ho' could stand for 'lo' or 'la'.
Combined pronouns go indirect before direct: 'me lo' = it to me, 'glielo' = it to him/her.
'Averne abbastanza' is a set phrase meaning to be fed up. 'Ne ho abbastanza' literally says I have enough of it.
In the 'tu' command, pronouns attach to the verb end: 'porta' plus 'me' plus 'la' becomes 'portamela', bring it to me.
When 'ne' refers to a masculine plural, the past participle agrees: 'ne ho comprati tre', not 'comprato'.
Before 'lo', 'la', 'li', 'le' or 'ne', the pronoun 'ti' changes to 'te': 'te lo mando' means I send it to you.
Pronouns attach to an infinitive, which drops its final -e: 'portare' plus 'li' becomes 'portarli', carry them.
'Aspettare' takes its object directly, with no word for for: 'vi abbiamo aspettato' means we waited for you.
'Per' plus an infinitive expresses purpose, in order to: 'lavora per guadagnare', he works in order to earn.
'Mi' already means to me, so no preposition is needed: 'mi ha detto' is literally he told to me.
For an action still going on, Italian uses the present with 'da': 'abito qui da cinque anni', I have lived here five years.
After a preposition, use 'cui' and not 'che': 'la ragione per cui' means the reason for which, the reason why.
'Il quale', 'la quale', 'i quali', 'le quali' can replace 'che' and agree in gender and number: 'la quale' points to a feminine noun.
'Aspettarsi', with 'mi', means to expect, unlike plain 'aspettare', to wait for: 'mi aspettavo' means I expected.
'È necessario che' takes the subjunctive: 'venga', not 'vieni'.
'Affinché', meaning so that, always takes the subjunctive: 'affinché tutto vada bene', not 'va'.
A possessive with one close family member usually drops the article: 'mia sorella', not 'la mia sorella'.
'Even though' words like 'nonostante' force the subjunctive: 'faccia caldo', not 'fa caldo'.
When the subjects differ, 'volere che' takes the subjunctive: 'voglio che mio fratello venga', not 'viene'.
'Vorremmo' is the conditional of 'volere' and means we would like: softer and more polite than the blunt 'vogliamo' (we want).
'Nonostante' forces the subjunctive even for a plain fact: 'sia stanco' means I'm tired, though English changes nothing.
Impersonal judgments like 'è meglio che' demand the subjunctive: 'tu faccia', where English just says you do.
'Voler bene a qualcuno' means to care about someone; save 'ti amo' for romantic love. Here: 'ti voglio bene'.
'Stare' plus the -ndo form marks an action in progress right now: 'sto leggendo' = I am reading.
'Farcela' is a set idiom meaning to manage or pull it off; the 'ce' and 'la' never change: 'ce la facciamo'.
With 'piacere' the liked thing is the subject, so it literally reads it is pleasing to me: 'non mi piace'.
'Aspettare' takes a direct object with no word for for: 'vi stiamo aspettando' = we are waiting for you.
